title: 1 Chronicles 4:1–10
context: The Chronicler returns to Judah, the tribe he treats first and at greatest length, and adds further clans to the lines already traced in chapter 2. The opening list appears to follow a line of descent rather than five brothers, since elsewhere Hezron is the son of Perez (2:5) and Hur and Shobal belong to later generations (2:19, 50). Short notes on clans, towns, and founders follow, many of them place names whose locations are uncertain. In the middle stands Jabez (4:9–10), a man more honorable than his brothers who called on the God of Israel and was answered. Arminian and Reformed readers alike take the Jabez notice in its genealogical setting: a brief record of a man who prayed and of God’s free answer, not a formula for success.

verses.text: The sons of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Chronicler opening this second pass through Judah by gathering names that tie the tribe back to Judah himself. The list seems to compress several generations (compare 2:5, 19, 50), and the point is continuity: the families of Judah, scattered through many settlements, still belong to one covenant people with a real history before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the compressed line of descent and read it as part of the Chronicler’s careful tracing of the royal tribe. Both traditions agree that the names serve a theological purpose for a restored community, reminding them that God had preserved Judah’s families across the generations and kept the line from which David’s house came.

verses.text: Reaiah the son of Shobal became the father of Jahath; and Jahath became the father of Ahumai and Lahad. These are the families of the Zorathites.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Reaiah, Jahath, Ahumai, and Lahad are otherwise little known, yet the Chronicler records them and names the Zorathites as a family group. The verse shows that ordinary households, not only kings and heroes, had a place in Israel’s remembered story and in the people whom God had called to himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same care for obscure names as a mark of God’s faithfulness to every household within the covenant people. Both traditions can affirm that the Zorathites are mentioned without any recorded deeds, and that their inclusion reflects the Chronicler’s conviction that belonging to Israel rests on God’s dealings with the whole people, not on fame.

verses.text: These were the sons of the father of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash. The name of their sister was Hazzelelponi.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the phrase about the father of Etam probably refers to a founder or leading figure of a settlement, a common way these lists speak, though the exact sense is uncertain. The mention of a sister, Hazzelelponi, by name is a small reminder that women were part of the remembered families of Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also take father of a town as likely describing a founder or head, while acknowledging that the details cannot be pressed. Both traditions value the naming of a daughter in a list largely made of sons, and both read the verse as part of the Chronicler’s picture of a people whose many households were known and preserved.

verses.text: Penuel was the father of Gedor and Ezer the father of Hushah. These are the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the link to Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, and to Bethlehem, the town later bound up with David. Without overreading the connection, the verse reminds the restored community that the places of their history were tied to families God had sustained, and that their own homes stood within that longer story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly hear in the mention of Bethlehem a quiet anticipation of David’s house, which the Chronicler will soon make central. Both traditions agree that the verse does not develop the theme but places it in the record, showing that the families of Judah and the towns they founded lay within God’s ongoing purpose for his people.

verses.text: Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ashhur, the father of Tekoa, introduced with his two wives, a detail recorded without comment. The Chronicler is tracing households as they actually were, and the list gives no moral verdict on the arrangement; it simply preserves the families from which later generations of Tekoa traced their descent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the text reports the two wives without endorsing or condemning the arrangement, consistent with the way genealogies record family structures. Both traditions agree that the point here is lineage and settlement, and that God’s preservation of the families of Tekoa is the thread the Chronicler wishes readers to follow.

verses.text: Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the sons of Naarah are named and then summed up, a typical pattern in these lists. Each name represents a household whose members would have heard this record as part of their own identity, and the verse shows the Chronicler’s concern that no branch of Judah be forgotten.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the careful listing of Naarah’s sons the Chronicler’s conviction that God keeps account of his people by name. Both traditions can affirm that these otherwise unknown names matter in the record because they belong to the covenant people, and that the summary line underscores the completeness the Chronicler seeks.

verses.text: The sons of Helah were Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the sons of Helah complete Ashhur’s household, so that both wives’ children are recorded. The balance shows the Chronicler’s attention to the whole family, and it reminds readers that God’s people are made up of many households, each with its own place and history in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the completion of Ashhur’s line and see in it the careful record of a people preserved by God. Both traditions agree that the verse adds no narrative but contributes to the larger purpose of the genealogies: to show the returned community that its roots run deep and that God has kept faith with its families.

verses.text: Hakkoz became the father of Anub, Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Hakkoz and the families of Aharhel appear briefly, with no stated connection to the names before them. The Chronicler seems to be gathering fragments of family memory, and the verse shows that even partial records were worth preserving for a people seeking to understand their place before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also recognize that the connection of Hakkoz to the preceding lines is not stated and should not be forced. Both traditions see the Chronicler preserving what the records held, honoring the families of Aharhel as part of Judah, and trusting that God’s faithfulness to his people extends to households whose stories are largely unknown.

verses.text: Jabez was more honorable than his brothers. His mother named him Jabez, saying, “Because I bore him with sorrow.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Jabez is introduced as more honorable than his brothers, and that his name is explained by his mother’s sorrow in bearing him. The name carries a sound of pain, and the verse sets up a life that began under a shadow; what follows shows him turning to God rather than resigning himself to that beginning. A place called Jabez also appears in 2:55, though the text does not say whether the two are connected.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe that the verse gives Jabez an honorable standing without explaining its basis, and that his name recalls his mother’s pain. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler pauses the list to tell a short story, and that the honor ascribed to Jabez is best read in light of the prayer that follows rather than as a separate achievement.

verses.text: Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, “Oh that you would bless me indeed, and enlarge my border! May your hand be with me, and may you keep me from evil, that I may not cause pain!” God granted him that which he requested.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Jabez as a man who called on the God of Israel with honest requests: blessing, a larger border, God’s hand with him, and protection from evil so that he would not cause pain. The notice that God granted his request presents a real relationship in which prayer is heard and answered. Arminian readers caution, as Reformed readers do, against turning this brief notice into a formula that guarantees prosperity to anyone who repeats the words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm the same plain point: Jabez prayed to the God of Israel and God granted what he asked. They emphasize that the answer was God’s free gift, given according to his own goodness, and that the prayer itself asks for God’s presence and protection as much as for land. Both traditions read the verse in its genealogical setting as an encouragement to call on God, and both reject treating it as a technique for securing material success.
